ADD 0000 arithmetic

Addition +

Binary addition with carry-out, built from a chain of full adders.

Flags affected ZCNV

Addition is the operation the rest of the ALU is often built around — a subtractor is usually just an adder fed an inverted second operand. A 4-bit adder is four full adders chained together, each one passing its carry-out to the next bit’s carry-in.

Truth table for one bit

Each full adder takes three inputs — the two operand bits and a carry-in — and produces a sum bit and a carry-out.

Two ways to wire the carry chain

Chaining full adders is simple to build, but that simplicity has a cost: each stage has to wait for the carry from the stage before it. Real ALUs weigh that cost against a more complex circuit that computes every carry sooner.

Ripple-carry adder. Stage i can’t produce its carry-out until stage i − 1 has produced its carry-out — the carry ripples down the chain one full adder at a time. It’s the fewest gates, but the worst-case delay grows with the width of the adder: a 64-bit ripple-carry adder is roughly sixteen times slower than a 4-bit one.

Carry-lookahead adder. Instead of waiting on its neighbor, every stage computes two signals up front — generate (G = A · B, “this stage makes a carry no matter what”) and propagate (P = A ⊕ B, “this stage passes a carry through if one arrives”). A separate block of gates combines all the G and P signals directly against the carry-in to produce every carry bit in parallel, in a fixed number of gate delays no matter how wide the adder is. The trade is more gates and more wiring for that flat delay.

Switch between the two below and watch the carry chain settle — ripple-carry lights up one node at a time, left to right; carry-lookahead lights the whole chain up in a single step.

Reading the flags

  • Z — set when all four result bits are 0.
  • C — set when the top bit’s adder produces a carry-out, meaning the true sum didn’t fit in 4 bits.
  • N — set when the result’s top bit is 1 (its sign bit, if you’re treating the result as a signed number).
  • V — set when the signed result is wrong even though the unsigned bits are correct — for example, adding two positive 4-bit numbers and landing on a negative-looking result.
